To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the LFP in macaque TE is linear; and 2) there is both uni- and bidirectional coupling in macaque TE.

1) LFPs in macaque area TE can be described by a simple linear model with a lagged input; 2) this linear model reveals uni- and bi- directionality of interactions; 3) the linear model is a special case of a more general model that is non-linear; 4) the non-linear model can be used to test for non-lineariy and to test for directedness of interactions.

(1) LFPs in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex are well described by a linear autoregressive (AR) model with lagged values of up to about 60 ms; (2) the non-linearity test based on LLNARS indicates that the data are not significantly better described by a non-linear than a linear model; (3) the Granger causality test indicates that there are uni- and bi- directional influences between recording sites in the IT cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the analysis of neurophysiological data.
the development of methods for modelling the dynamics of neural interactions.
the development of methods that are capable of disentangling complex patterns of neural interactions in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

linear models of the form of the linear LLNAR are sufficient for the data at hand, but the non-linear variant of LLNARS is needed to capture the full richness of the data and to allow for a full description of the functional connectivity between the recording sites.
linear and instantaneous interactions are not sufficient to describe the dynamics of neural interactions in the visual cortex.
the linear model of LLNAR is the most appropriate model to describe the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the linear variant of the LLNAR model is sufficient for describing local field potentials in the macaque temporal cortex.
the LFP data is best described by linear models and that these linear models reveal both uni- and bidirectional influences between neural groups.
the LLNAR model can be used to describe the LFP data in a way that allows the detection of linear and non-linear interactions between neuronal populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of linear models for the analysis of LFP data is justified, at least for macaque inferotemproal cortex.
LLNAR provides a general framework for modelling neurophysiological data, which allows to test for non-linearties and to measure directional influences in a principled way.
non-linear interactions between neural groups can be detected by means of LLNAR, and that this approach can be applied to LFP data.
